### The Dutch pension transition, as the worked example


> **[Level 1 · First principles]**
>
> Dutch pension funds are moving from a system that promised a fixed pension to one where each member has a personal pot managed by age group. A promise needs protecting against falling interest rates, so the old funds held very large interest-rate hedges. A young member's pot does not need that protection. So as funds convert, some of that hedging is no longer needed and the growth portfolios are redesigned.


*[Layer A · verified fact]* Thirty Dutch pension funds holding about €542bn had converted by 31 March 2026, most of them on 1 January 2026. The rest must transfer accrued entitlements by 1 January 2028. *[Verified]* [R5-S35][R5-S36]

| Step | Dutch pension transition |
|---|---|
| What happened | Largest conversion wave on 1 January 2026 (reported April 2026). Deadline 1 January 2028. |
| Client effect | Funds manage pots by age cohort. Hedging and return portfolios are rebuilt. |
| Decision that changes | How much interest-rate hedging each cohort keeps, and what replaces it. |
| Existing investments | Long-dated bonds and swaps may be reduced. Return-seeking allocations are redesigned. |
| Possible GSAM response *[Layer B · interpretation]* | Cohort-aware fixed income and return building blocks, with analysis specific to each fund's design. |
| Sales responsibility | Native-language coverage of funds and of the fiduciary managers many of them use. |
| Relationship management responsibility | Keep existing mandates aligned with the fund's new design through its conversion date. |
| Risks and counterarguments | The January 2026 wave passed calmly, so the forced-selling story may be overstated. Estimates of future hedge reduction come from interested parties. *[Supported inference]* [R5-S37] Many funds delegate to a fiduciary manager, so the buyer is one step removed. |

| Element | View (forecasts labelled) |
|---|---|
| Base case (forecast) | Remaining funds convert by the deadline and hedging demand falls gradually, cohort by cohort. |
| Plausible alternatives | Conversions are delayed. Or several large funds cut hedges at once and long-dated euro rates move sharply. |
| Indicators to watch | The number and size of funds converting each January. The Dutch central bank's transition reporting. |
| Evidence that would change the view | A formal extension of the deadline. Funds publishing higher post-conversion hedge ratios than expected. |

### 10.4 Replacing slogans with consequences

"Global platform" and "strong reputation" could be said of ten firms. A statement worth making names a capability, the evidence, and the consequence for one type of client.

| Slogan | A specific version | The honest qualifier |
|---|---|---|
| "Global platform" | "A UK scheme delegating its whole portfolio gets liability hedging, external manager selection and private-market access from one accountable provider, at a firm that reports over $540bn of OCIO assets." | "Several rivals offer the same combination, and trustees should ask how in-house funds are chosen over external ones." |
| "Strong in alternatives" | "A private bank can list an evergreen private-credit vehicle and an active ETF from the same coverage relationship." | "Blackstone's wealth franchise is far larger, and 2026 showed these funds can limit redemptions." |
| "Strong reputation" | "The trustees of a £23bn scheme appointed it after a competitive tender in which they were advised by an independent investment adviser." | "One appointment shows it can win a tender. It does not show how the mandate has performed since." |
| "Leader in liquidity" | "Over a trillion dollars of liquidity products firm-wide, which supports diversification and same-day dealing." | "The sterling and euro fund ranking was not found, so 'leader' is not a claim to make." |

## 11. The future of the work

This section separates what has been observed from what is a scenario. It analyses tasks, because whole roles rarely disappear and individual tasks often do.

### 11.1 Observed changes and scenarios, kept apart

| Theme | Observed (with source) | Scenario (not observed) |
|---|---|---|
| AI in distribution | 81% of institutional sales and service teams use AI for RFP content and 77% for meeting notes; far fewer for prospecting (26% to 32%). *[Verified]* [R8-S41] Only 5% of managers let AI act with any autonomy on recommendations or trades. *[Verified]* [R8-S42] | AI choosing which clients to pursue. Client-ready material sent with no human sign-off. |
| Fee pressure | Institutional fees falling about 3% a year; over 80% of 2025 revenue growth came from markets; costs grew faster than revenue from 2010 to 2025. *[Verified]* [R8-S38] Goldman Sachs's own effective fee was 31 basis points in 2025 and it lists further decline as a risk. *[Verified]* [R2-S01] | Fees stabilising as mix shifts to private assets. Or a market fall exposing cost bases. |
| Passive investing | In Europe active equity funds still held more than passive at the first quarter of 2026, but passive ETFs took about 57% of flows in the third quarter. *[Supported inference]* [R8-S39] | Active becoming a specialist allocation everywhere. |
| Private markets | Goldman Sachs raised $122bn of alternatives commitments in nine months of 2026. *[Verified]* [R2-S02] Retail fund redemptions were elevated. *[Verified]* [R8-S52] | Semi-liquid funds becoming standard in model portfolios. Or a gating episode reversing demand. |
| Intermediary change | Model portfolios concentrating selection. *[Supported inference]* [R4-S37] Consultants consolidating. *[Supported inference]* [R3-S34] | A handful of gatekeepers controlling most wealth flows. |
| Pension consolidation | DC scale test legislated; LGPS down to six pools. *[Verified]* [R3-S20][R3-S21] | A UK market with a few dozen institutional buyers that matter. |
| Industry structure | About $53.8bn of asset-manager mergers in the year to August 2026. *[Supported inference]* [R8-S54] Reported job cuts at several large managers. *[Supported inference]* [R8-S47][R8-S48] | AI-driven cuts to entry-level client-facing hiring. No credible data on this was found. *[Not publicly established]* |

### 11.2 Task by task

| Task | What is being automated (observed) | What still needs a person | What is uncertain | Effect on junior learning *[Layer B · interpretation]* |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| RFP and DDQ first drafts | Drafting answers and searching content libraries. *[Verified]* [R8-S41] | Checking every answer against approved, current content. Invented answers are the most cited barrier. *[Supported inference]* [R8-S44] | Whether clients respond by issuing longer questionnaires. | Less writing from scratch, more verifying. The skill moves from drafting to judging accuracy. |
| Meeting notes | Note-taking and summaries. *[Verified]* [R8-S41] | Deciding what was agreed, what is sensitive, who must act. | Client consent and confidentiality practice. | A task that taught listening is partly automated. The learning has to come from attending and being questioned afterwards. |
| Routine reports and emails | Drafting reports and emails; 85% of UK fiduciary managers use AI mainly for this. *[Verified]* [R8-S10] | Reconciling numbers, attribution, and tone when performance is poor. | Regulators' expectations on accountability. | Less time building packs, more responsibility for checking them. |
| Prospecting and planning | Low adoption so far. *[Verified]* [R8-S41] | Relationship context, suitability, whether to pursue at all. | Whether adoption is low or merely early. | Client research remains a junior task, with better tools. |
| Investment decisions | AI used in at least one process at over half of managers; almost none let it decide. *[Verified]* [R8-S42] | Portfolio managers remain the decision-makers. | Pace of change. | Not a coverage task, but coverage staff must explain how AI is used. |
| Headcount | One consultancy estimates AI could cut industry costs 25% to 35% over three to five years. That is an estimate. *[Verified]* [R8-S38] | Not applicable. | No data links AI to entry-level distribution hiring. *[Not publicly established]* | If preparation work shrinks, firms may hire fewer juniors or expect earlier client exposure. Both are scenarios. |

### 11.3 Where people add measurable value, and where technology may do better

It would be easy to write "relationships cannot be automated". That is a slogan. A more defensible version separates the cases.

**Where technology is likely to do better.** Retrieving the approved answer to a standard question. Producing the first draft of a recurring report. Summarising a long document. Noticing that a client has not been contacted for six months. These are tasks where speed, recall and consistency matter and where a mistake is caught by review.

**Where a person adds value that can be observed.**

- *Accountability.* A named person signs what is sent to a client and answers for it. One industry analyst put it as AI being "unable to replace the credibility that comes from well-crafted and verified human communication". *[Verified]* [R8-S41] That is one analyst's judgement, not a law.
- *Finding out what was not written down.* A request for proposal says what the trustees agreed to ask. It does not say which trustee is unconvinced or what went wrong with the last manager. That comes from conversation.
- *Deciding not to proceed.* Judging that a product does not suit a client, or that a prospect is two years from buyout and should not be pursued, is a judgement with a commercial cost attached.
- *Delivering bad news.* Explaining poor performance to a board that must then explain it to members.

**Where it is uncertain.** Whether clients will come to prefer a faster, cheaper, more automated service for routine matters and reserve people for the difficult moments. If so, the number of coverage people needed per client falls even though the value of each good one rises.


> **[Limits and caveats: The apprenticeship problem]**
>
> *[Layer B · interpretation]* Many junior tasks that are being automated (first drafts, notes, packs) were also how people learned the business. If those shrink, a junior person learns less by doing unless the firm replaces them with something else: earlier attendance at meetings, more responsibility for checking, structured questioning by seniors. A fair interview question to ask is how the team trains analysts now that drafting is assisted.


### 11.4 What is established about Goldman Sachs's own AI tools

The former intern said Goldman "recently restricted staff use of Claude Code". The public record is narrower and should be stated precisely.

- Goldman Sachs launched its own "GS AI Assistant" firm-wide in June 2025, with versions for different staff groups including asset and wealth management. *[Verified]* [R2-S13]
- Reuters reported on 28 April 2026 that Goldman removed its Hong Kong bankers' access to one external model on its internal platform, with other models still available. Goldman declined to comment. *[Verified]* [R2-S12]
- Bloomberg News published an article on 2 November 2026 headed "Goldman Restricts Traders and Bankers From Using Some AI Tools". *[Verified]* [R2-S10] The article itself was not read. Two outlets that summarised it report that internal guidance limited certain AI coding tools to engineers, removing access from bankers, traders and most other staff. *[Supported inference]* [R2-S08][R2-S09]
- A reported October 2025 internal memo named sales and client onboarding among processes targeted for AI-driven redesign and said headcount growth would be constrained. *[Supported inference]* [R8-S45]

What this does **not** establish: a firm-wide ban on any AI model, anything specific to asset-management client staff, or the reasons. *[Not publicly established]* The safe statement is: "Press reports say Goldman narrowed access to some AI coding tools to engineers in autumn 2026, while it runs its own internal assistant for all staff. I have not seen the firm's policy."


> **[Check your understanding]**
>
> - Name one coverage task where technology is likely to do better than a person and one where a person adds observable value. Give the reason for each.
> - State the Goldman AI-tools finding in two sentences without overstating it.
> - What would you want to know about how a team trains analysts when drafting is assisted?


## 12. Using this chapter without overreaching

- **Lead with the client, not the event.** "A scheme at 130% funded is choosing an endgame, and the Act changes what run-on is worth" is stronger than "the Pension Schemes Act passed".
- **Date everything.** "As of the November decision, Bank Rate is 4%."
- **Offer the counterargument yourself.** It shows the conclusion was tested.
- **Say what you do not know.** Goldman's UK market shares, fee rates and team structures are largely not public. Saying so is more credible than guessing.
- **Do not assume a sale.** For each development, be ready to say when the right response is to explain, to wait, or to help the client reduce what it holds with you.


> **[Check your understanding]**
>
> - Choose one team. State its base case, one alternative, and the single indicator you would watch.
> - For that team, name a development that is not a reason to sell anything, and say what the right response is.
> - Which three facts in this chapter are most likely to be out of date first, and where would you check them?

# Interview understanding and practice

This chapter turns the research into practice. It comes last on purpose. An answer is the visible end of an argument, and the argument rests on facts about the business and on evidence about you. If either is missing, a fluent answer will fail at the first follow-up question.


> **[Limits and caveats: What this chapter can and cannot do]**
>
> The six criteria used here are a **proposed practice framework** written for this project. Goldman Sachs has not published scoring criteria for this programme, and nobody outside the firm knows which questions will be asked. *[Not publicly established]* Everything in the question bank is plausible practice material, not a prediction.
> 
> This material is for preparation **before** an assessment. Do not use it, or any tool, during a live or recorded interview. The practice mode in the application shows a silent timer only. It records nothing and sends nothing anywhere.
> 
> No personal history has been written for you. Wherever an answer needs your own experience, the bank shows a slot in square brackets, such as "[my own example: a time I …]". Only you can fill it, and an honest "I have not tested this yet" is a valid way to fill it.


## What is publicly known about the process

Keep the verified facts apart from what you have been told.

*[Layer A · verified fact]* Goldman's careers site describes a first-round video interview of about 30 minutes, which it refers to as the HireVue interview, and a final round called a Superday of typically two to five interviews with people the candidate could work with. [R1-S23] *[Verified]* The summer programme runs for nine to ten weeks. [R1-S22] *[Verified]* An applicant may apply to at most four business and location combinations in a recruiting year. [R1-S02] *[Verified]*

*[Layer A · verified fact]* The official London listing for this programme contains no duties, team names or language requirements specific to the Client Solutions Group. Its text is programme-wide and division-wide. [R1-S02] *[Verified]*

Several things the former intern said are not publicly established: that the content of a recorded answer decides which team you are sent to, that an associate reviews the video at double speed, the exact order of interviewers, and that assessment centres will ask more about AI. *[Unverified account]* They may be true. They are one person's experience from an earlier cycle.


> **[Limits and caveats: Do not build tactics on unverified claims]**
>
> It is tempting to mention a region or a product in a recorded answer because someone said it steers you to a team. Do not. The claim is unverified, the tactic produces an answer you cannot defend ("why the Middle East?"), and it replaces a real preference with a guess about a sorting rule. Say what you actually find interesting and why. If you have a constraint, such as speaking only English, say that too: several regional teams state a language requirement in their adverts. [R1-S01] *[Verified]*


## Why answers come after understanding

A memorised answer has one layer. An interviewer who wants to know whether you understand something asks a second question, and the second question is never the one you memorised.

Compare two candidates asked "Why Goldman Sachs?". The first says the firm has a global platform and a culture of excellence. The interviewer asks, "What would be different at BlackRock?" and there is nothing underneath. The second says that the asset management business serves institutions and intermediaries at scale and runs whole-portfolio mandates, gives one dated fact, and says plainly that other firms have breadth too. The same follow-up now has somewhere to go, because the candidate already knows where the claim is weak.

The difference is not vocabulary or confidence. The second candidate did three things before the interview:

1. Learned what the business does and how it is paid (Chapter 1 and the chapters on the role, the teams and the economics).
2. Worked out which of their own claims are supported and which are hopes (the why-trees and the ledger in [Chapter 8](#ch08)).
3. Practised saying it aloud, in time, to the standard below.


> **[Level 1 · First principles]**
>
> **In plain terms.** You are not trying to produce good sentences. You are trying to hold a position you can explain, defend and, where necessary, give ground on. The sentences follow.


## Building an answer from an argument

Every substantial answer in the bank is built from the same five parts. You will not always say all five aloud, but you should have all five ready.

| Part | What it is | The test it must pass |
|---|---|---|
| Claim | One sentence that answers the question asked | Could a listener repeat it? |
| Mechanism | Why the claim is true: how the thing works | Does it explain, or only assert? |
| Evidence | A verified fact with its date, or a real event from your own life | Could someone check it? |
| Limit | Where the claim stops being true, or what a competitor could also say | Have you said it before the interviewer does? |
| Personal link | Why this matters to you, backed by something that happened | Is it evidence or an adjective? |


> **[Illustrative example: Building "Why asset management?" from the five parts]**
>
> **Claim.** I am drawn to how asset management is paid: a fee on assets that continues only while the client chooses to stay.
> 
> **Mechanism.** That makes the relationship continuous. The manager is judged every quarter against something measurable, and the client's problem (a pension paid for decades) is long-term.
> 
> **Evidence.** In 2025, management and other fees were $11,538m of the $16,679m net revenues of Goldman's Asset & Wealth Management segment. [R2-S01] *[Verified]*
> 
> **Limit.** Fee revenue falls when markets fall, whatever anyone does. People in client coverage do not control the investment result. A lot of early work is preparation.
> 
> **Personal link.** [My own example: a long-running responsibility I stayed with, and what kept me interested.] If I have none, I say that this is a reasoned preference I am applying in order to test.


The order matters less than the completeness. In a 30-second answer you might give the claim, one piece of mechanism and the limit. In a 60 to 90-second answer you add the evidence and the personal link. The longer version is not the short one with more words. It adds reasoning that was missing.


> **[Level 2 · Institutional mechanics]**
>
> **Why the limit earns more than it costs.** *[Layer B · interpretation]* Stating the limit of your own claim feels like weakening it. In practice it does three things. It shows you understand the claim well enough to know its edge. It removes the interviewer's easiest follow-up. And it is direct evidence of the behaviour the job needs: telling a client where a product does not fit ([Chapter 7](#ch07), "Trust, translated into behaviour"). A candidate who cannot find the limit of "why this firm" is unlikely to find the limit of a strategy in front of a trustee.
> 
> **Where facts go.** Use at most one or two figures in a spoken answer, each with its date. Figures are there to make a claim checkable, not to show how many you have learned. If you are not sure of a number, give the order of magnitude and say so, or leave it out.


## The six practice criteria

Score every practice attempt from 0 to 3 on each criterion. These are this project's proposal, chosen because each one corresponds to something the work itself requires. Confidence is deliberately not on the list.

| Criterion | What a 0 looks like | What a 3 looks like |
|---|---|---|
| Accuracy | A wrong fact, an invented figure, or a firm term misused ("asset management is 30% of revenue") | Facts correct and dated; the firm's own terms used properly; unknowns stated as unknown |
| Specificity | Every sentence would fit any employer or any client-facing job | Names a task, a client constraint or a verified fact, and survives "a competitor could say that too" |
| Logic | A list of assertions with no "because" | Claim, mechanism, evidence and limit follow in order, with no circular step |
| Judgement | One-sided; or gives a junior person a senior's authority | States the counterargument, the trade-off and who actually decides |
| Clarity | Jargon, hedging or running over time | One idea per sentence; a listener with no notes could repeat the main point |
| Supported personal evidence | Adjectives about yourself, or a motive borrowed from a guide | A specific true example, or a plain statement that the preference is untested |

Three notes on scoring yourself honestly:

- **Accuracy is pass or fail in spirit.** One confident factual error in front of someone who works there outweighs a good structure. The correction from "asset management is about 30% of Goldman's revenue" to "the Asset & Wealth Management segment was 28.6% of 2025 net revenues, and Asset management inside it was 11.6%" [R2-S01] *[Verified]* is the kind of precision that separates understanding from repetition.
- **A 3 for personal evidence can be an admission.** "I have not done this work, so this is what I expect to like and want to test" scores higher than an unsupported story.
- **Do not average away a zero.** A zero on accuracy or judgement is the thing to fix before the next attempt.

## Three worked transformations

Each example starts from a realistic weak answer, diagnoses it against the criteria, and rebuilds it. Notice that the improved answer is not always longer.

### 1. "Why Goldman Sachs?"


> **[Realistic conversation (illustrative): Weak version]**
>
> "Goldman Sachs is the most prestigious firm on the street, with a global platform, a strong culture of excellence and the best people. I have always wanted to work here and I know I would learn from the best."


**Diagnosis.** Specificity 0: every clause fits any large bank. Logic 0: nothing explains why any of it matters for client coverage. Personal evidence 0: "always wanted to" cannot be checked. Accuracy is untested because there are no facts to be wrong about, which is its own problem.

**What is missing.** A capability, evidence for it, why it changes the work, and its limit.


> **[Realistic conversation (illustrative): Better version (about 80 words)]**
>
> "Two things, both about the work. The asset management business serves institutions and wealth intermediaries at scale, and it runs public markets, alternatives, liquidity and whole-portfolio OCIO mandates under one roof. For someone starting in client coverage, that should mean the client's problem sets the conversation instead of one product. I can't claim that is unique to Goldman. I can say it is the setting I think I would learn most in, and I'd like to test that."


**Why it is better.** It names capabilities that can be evidenced: long-term assets under supervision of $1,245bn institutional and $714bn third-party distributed at 30 September 2026 [R2-S02] *[Verified]*, and $480bn of OCIO assets at 31 March 2026 [R3-S09] *[Verified]*. It links them to what a junior would experience, and it labels that link as an inference. It concedes the limit before being asked. If pressed for proof, the BAE Systems appointment of about £23bn after a competitive tender is public. [R3-S01] *[Verified]*

**What it still depends on.** The last sentence is a personal claim. You need a real reason why problem-led work across client types appeals to you. Full treatment: [IQ-01](#IQ-01) and [IQ-02](#IQ-02).

### 2. "What would you actually do as an analyst?"


> **[Realistic conversation (illustrative): Weak version]**
>
> "I'd be building relationships with clients, pitching investment solutions and helping to win new mandates for the firm from day one."


**Diagnosis.** Judgement 0: it gives an intern a senior's job. Accuracy 0: interns do not pitch to clients or win mandates. It also hints that the candidate will be disappointed by the real work.


> **[Realistic conversation (illustrative): Better version (about 70 words)]**
>
> "Mostly preparation and follow-through. Researching a client before a meeting and writing the briefing note. Pulling the numbers for a quarterly review pack and checking them. Drafting parts of a due-diligence response. Keeping the pipeline and client records accurate. Taking notes and chasing actions. I wouldn't be advising clients or quoting anything. The point of the work is that the senior people are properly prepared and what was promised gets done."


**Why it is better.** It is concrete, it is modest about decision rights, and it explains why unglamorous work matters. It should be offered with one honest caveat: the published London listing does not describe team duties [R1-S02] *[Verified]*, so this list is a supported inference from team adverts [R1-S01] and general practice ([Chapter 6](#ch06), "What each level of seniority realistically contributes"). *[Supported inference]* Saying so costs nothing and shows you know the status of your own knowledge. Full treatment: [IQ-14](#IQ-14).

### 3. "You have explained why the role matters. Why would you enjoy it?"

This is the example where the better answer is shorter and plainer than the weak one could have been.


> **[Realistic conversation (illustrative): Weak version]**
>
> "I'd enjoy it because I'm passionate about helping clients achieve their goals, and there's nothing more rewarding than knowing you've made a difference. I thrive in fast-paced environments, I love building relationships, and I'm excited by the chance to work at the intersection of markets and people."


**Diagnosis.** The question excluded "why it matters", and the answer gives it again. Personal evidence 0: five self-descriptions, no event. Specificity 0: it would suit nursing, teaching or recruitment.


> **[Realistic conversation (illustrative): Better version]**
>
> "Fair challenge. Important and enjoyable aren't the same. The parts I think I'd enjoy are specific: working out how an unfamiliar organisation makes decisions, and getting a piece of written work exactly right for someone else to use. My evidence is [my own example]. The part I expect to find hard is repetition, the fifth quarterly pack. I can't prove I'd enjoy it until I've done it, which is partly why I'm applying."


**Why it is better.** It accepts the distinction, names tasks, offers evidence, names a cost and admits uncertainty. It contains no adjective about the speaker. If the slot is empty, the answer still works: "I don't have strong evidence yet. Here is why I expect to, and here is what would tell me I was wrong." Full treatment: [IQ-31](#IQ-31), and the section "A valuable role is not the same as a role I would enjoy" in [Chapter 8](#ch08).

## How to handle "I don't know"

You will be asked something you cannot answer. That is partly the point: the job involves being asked such questions by clients, and the interviewer may be more interested in what you do next than in the answer.


> **[Level 1 · First principles]**
>
> There are three situations, and each has its own honest response.
> 
> **You do not know a fact.** Say so, then offer what you do know and how you would find out. "I don't know the current figure. The last number I saw was the end of September, about 4.1 trillion dollars of assets under supervision. I'd check the latest earnings release."
> 
> **You do not know how something works.** Say so, then reason from what you understand. "I haven't come across that. From what I know about how schemes hedge, I'd guess it works like this. Is that close?" A labelled guess that shows reasoning is fine. An unlabelled guess is not.
> 
> **You do not know your own mind.** Say so. "I don't yet know whether I'd prefer the sales or the servicing side. Here is what draws me to each, and here is what I'd need to see to find out."



> **[Realistic conversation (illustrative): Words that work]**
>
> "I'm not sure, and I'd rather not guess."
> 
> "I know part of that. The part I'm confident about is … The part I'd need to check is …"
> 
> "I haven't thought about it from that angle. Can I take a moment?"
> 
> "I got that wrong a minute ago. What I should have said is …"



> **[Limits and caveats: What to avoid]**
>
> - **Confident invention.** A made-up figure or mechanism, delivered smoothly. It is the single most damaging thing you can do, because it shows the interviewer what you would do with a client.
> - **The vague retreat.** "It depends on a lot of factors" with none named.
> - **Changing the subject** to something you prepared.
> - **Over-apologising.** One plain sentence is enough.


Correcting yourself is also allowed. If you realise mid-answer that you misstated something, stop and fix it. People who work with clients do this every week.

## What not to do

**Keyword tactics drawn from unverified recruitment claims.** Covered above. If you have been told that certain words send you to certain teams, or that reviewers skim at double speed, treat it as a rumour. Optimising for a rumour makes answers worse and cannot be defended.

**Confident invention.** Never state a Goldman fee, team size, internal structure, client name or interview criterion you cannot source. The team structure in particular: one person's informal account contains points that public sources contradict, such as OCIO being a UK-only team. [R3-S09] *[Conflicting evidence]* "I've heard an informal description but couldn't verify it" is a strong sentence.

**Borrowed motives.** If a line in this bank is not true of you, do not say it. The suggested answers are written in a provisional first person so that they can be adapted. They are not meant to be adopted. A motive you cannot support with one true example will fail the question "what's your evidence?".

**Naming clients you cannot source.** The BAE Systems appointment is public through the manager's own press release. [R3-S01] *[Verified]* A second company the former intern mentioned has no public confirmation, and scheme documents point elsewhere, so it is left out of every answer here. *[Not publicly established]* Repeating a client name described as confidential would show poor judgement about exactly the thing this job depends on.

**Ranking colleagues' work.** Do not call relationship management "admin", banking "brutal" or passive investing "lazy". You may be speaking to someone who does it.

**Lengthening instead of improving.** If an answer is weak, the fix is usually a missing mechanism or a missing limit. More words rarely help.

**Reading from notes or tools in the interview.** Besides being against the spirit of the assessment, it shows. The purpose of practice is that the argument is in your head.

## Using the practice mode

The application's practice mode draws a question, runs a silent timer and asks you to score yourself. A routine that works:

1. **Draw a question and answer aloud** before opening anything. Speaking exposes gaps that reading hides.
2. **Stop at the time limit.** About 70 to 80 words fills 30 seconds. About 170 to 220 words fills 60 to 90 seconds.
3. **Score all six criteria** before you reveal the reasoning. Be strict on accuracy and on personal evidence.
4. **Reveal the underlying argument** and compare. Look for the part you missed: usually the limit.
5. **Try one follow-up.** The follow-ups get harder. If the first one stops you, the understanding is thin, and the map below shows which chapter to reread.
6. **Record the attempt** if you want a history. Saving is off unless you turn it on, and it stays in your browser.

Work through the practice cases the same way. Each gives a situation, your realistic role in it, what good looks like and the traps. Say what you would do, then compare. In every case the junior's decision rights are limited on purpose: the skill being practised is noticing, checking, escalating and following through, not deciding for the client.


> **[Note: On the personal slots]**
>
> Before practising the motivation questions, fill in the personal ledger and reflection questions in [Chapter 8](#ch08). A slot answered with a small true example ("I kept a weekly report accurate for ten weeks and here is what I noticed") beats one answered with a large vague one.

The six practice cases draw on the same material: PC-01 and PC-02 on the economics and on Chapter 7's treatment of honesty; PC-03 on suitability and decision rights; PC-04 on admitting limits; PC-05 on responsiveness against accuracy; PC-06 on the wealth-intermediary chain.


> **[Level 2 · Institutional mechanics]**
>
> **How the hard follow-ups are constructed.** *[Layer B · interpretation]* Almost every difficult follow-up in the bank is one of six moves. Knowing them lets you test your own answers before anyone else does.
> 
> | Move | Example | What it tests |
> |---|---|---|
> | Generalise | "Couldn't you say that about any client-facing job?" | Specificity |
> | Compete | "Why Goldman Sachs rather than a competitor with similar products?" | Whether the claim survives comparison |
> | Personalise | "You have explained why the role matters. Why would you enjoy it?" | Evidence about you |
> | Concretise | "What would you actually do as an analyst?" | Realism about tasks and decision rights |
> | Reverse | "When would the client be right to leave?" | Judgement when the firm's interest and the client's diverge |
> | Disconfirm | "What would make you decide this career is not for you?" | Whether the motivation has been tested |
> 
> For any answer you prepare, apply all six moves yourself. If one of them leaves you with nothing to say, that is the part to work on.



> **[Check your understanding: Before you practise]**
>
> 1. Without looking, state the five parts of an answer and the test each must pass.
> 2. Which two criteria should you never average away, and why?
> 3. Give the corrected version of "asset management is about 30% of Goldman's revenue", with the year.
> 4. What are the three kinds of "I don't know", and what is the honest response to each?
> 5. Name one thing the former intern said about the process that you should not act on, and explain why acting on it would make your answers worse.
> 6. Pick any answer you have prepared and apply the six follow-up moves. Which one exposes a gap?
> 7. Which slots in the question bank can you fill today with a true example, and which must you answer with "I have not tested this yet"?

# Acceptance test, open questions and limits

This chapter holds the project to its own standard. It answers the nine acceptance questions from the brief, lists what is still unresolved, and shows topic by topic what was investigated and what was not.

## The nine acceptance questions

Each answer says where the evidence is and where the project falls short. "Yes" is only claimed where you can check it yourself by doing the test described.

| Question | Honest answer | How to check it yourself |
|---|---|---|
| Can a beginner explain the business without memorising jargon? | The material is there: chapter 1 teaches each idea from first principles before any acronym is used, and the glossary defines every term in plain English. Whether you can explain it is a test only you can run | Close the file and explain to someone outside finance how a pension scheme's money reaches an asset manager and how the manager is paid |
| Can the reader distinguish sales, relationship management and adjacent roles without oversimplifying? | Yes for the general industry picture (chapters 2 and 6, role comparison). For Goldman specifically, the published evidence shows the labels overlap, and the internal split is not public | Compare any two roles in the Role comparison view and say what each can decide alone |
| Can the reader connect a junior task to a client outcome and a commercial consequence? | Yes. Every lifecycle stage lists what the junior person produces and what good execution changes, and the sample work products show the documents | Pick the meeting preparation note in chapter 7 and trace it to the mandate's fee in the calculator |
| Are the organisational claims, people and mandates supported, not invented? | Supported where sources exist, and marked where they do not. Several posts have no publicly established holder, and no mandate is attributed to a London team because no source does so | Open any team, person or mandate and follow its source link |
| Can every statement about trust, relationships, value or passion be translated into an action, a difficult choice or a concrete preference? | Chapter 7 ends with a translation table that does this word by word. Passion is deliberately not asserted anywhere | Take any sentence containing "trust" in your own draft answers and replace it using the table |
| Can the motivation arguments withstand repeated questioning without becoming circular? | The nine why-trees are built so that each question challenges the previous answer and each tree ends in a stated preference, assumption or uncertainty. Your own answers are untested until you give them | Answer each level aloud before opening it. Note where you repeat yourself |
| Does the material distinguish a strong business argument from evidence of personal fit? | Yes, structurally. Layer B and Layer C are labelled apart, and the personal ledger is empty by design | Check that nothing in your answers uses "the role is valuable" as proof that you would enjoy it |
| Does it explain when a client should not buy, when a mandate should shrink and when a different career might fit better? | Yes: chapter 7 on when a relationship should end, the withdrawal cases in chapter 5, and the "different role" signal at the end of each why-tree | Find the three passages and summarise each in two sentences |

## Research coverage register

Each row is a topic from the brief. "Complete" means the planned sources were read. "Partial" means some evidence was found and more exists. "Searched, not established" means it was looked for and not found in public sources. "Not investigated" means nobody has looked yet.

## Open questions worth resolving before an interview

These are the gaps most likely to matter in conversation, with the fastest way to close each.

1. **The current London listing.** The exact 2027 London listing carried only programme-wide wording when it was read on a mirror, and it was no longer among the live campus listings on 14 November 2026 [R1-S03]. Check your own application portal for the wording and any team information it shows you.
2. **How Client Solutions Group and Client Coverage Group relate in London.** Both names are real. Their reporting relationship is not published. A neutral question to ask an interviewer: "How do the sales and client coverage roles divide the work on your team?"
3. **Who leads UK institutional coverage and UK & Ireland third-party wealth today.** Neither post has a publicly established current holder. A departure from the EMEA third-party wealth leadership was reported in April 2026, with no successor found in public sources.
4. **Which OCIO award the former intern saw.** Two 2026 awards fit. Do not name one as fact.
5. **Analyst pay.** The two figures in the starting account have no public support. Do not build any argument on them.
6. **The interview format this cycle.** Goldman publishes the general shape of its process. Whether this team's final round is in person, and what it asks about AI, is not established. Prepare for both.

## Limits of this project

- **It is not exhaustive.** The people directory is a sample of publicly visible professionals. The mandates register holds what was found in the time and search allowance available. Neither should be described as complete.
- **It is dated.** Every figure is correct to the date beside it. The rates backdrop changed in the week before the cutoff, which shows how quickly a commercial-awareness point can go stale.
- **It contains interpretation.** Layer B passages are arguments. A well-informed interviewer may disagree with some of them, and a reasoned disagreement is a good conversation to have.
- **It cannot assess you.** Practice scores are self-assessed against a proposed framework. Goldman Sachs has not published scoring criteria, and nobody outside the firm knows the questions.
- **It was partly written by automated research and drafting.** Every claim carries a source or a label so that you can check it. Open the source for anything you intend to say aloud.

## What was tested

The application and PDF were checked by an automated script and by inspecting rendered pages. The README lists every check and its result. In brief: navigation, search, filters, expandable sections, the fee calculator's arithmetic against an independent implementation, keyboard access, mobile layout, reduced-motion behaviour, and that the file makes no network requests. The PDF was rendered and its pages inspected for clipped text and broken tables.

No part of this project has been published or hosted. The HTML file is a local file. If you choose to share it, check the source register and the people directory first and decide what you are comfortable circulating.

# Appendix A: Teams and coverage

### Client Solutions Group (CSG) `T-csg`

- **Evidence status:** Verified
- **Where the name comes from:** Goldman Sachs's own name. Campus and experienced-hire listings use 'Client Solutions Group', 'Global Client Solutions Group', 'Client Solutions Group / Sales' and 'Client Solutions Group (Sales)' [R1-S10][R1-S04][R1-S09][R1-S13].
- **Kind of unit:** Umbrella client organisation of Goldman Sachs Asset Management (global)
- **In one paragraph:** The part of Goldman Sachs Asset Management that develops client relationships and delivers investment solutions to institutional and third-party wealth clients worldwide, across public and private asset classes. Goldman's own listings gloss it as 'Sales' and call it 'the sales organization', but at least one London CSG team is also described as managing existing relationships, so it is not new-business-only.
- **Former intern's account:** An umbrella term for everyone who speaks to clients, 'the equivalent of saying sales', covering sales, client relationship management and consultant relations, cut by coverage team, then client type, then sales versus relationship management. He also used 'CSG' for the sales side inside a team. [Unverified account]
- **What public sources establish:** Goldman describes CSG as developing client relationships and delivering investment solutions 'for institutional and third-party wealth clients across the globe' [R1-S10]. Listing titles equate it with sales [R1-S04][R1-S09][R1-S14]. It has a named head (Matt Gibson) [R6-S19] and its own management, strategy and finance team that runs sales budgeting, fundraising projections and Salesforce data governance [R1-S13][R1-S14]. A Goldman job advert lists the distribution channels as third party wealth, institutional, consultant, insurance and retirement [R4-S09]. CSG roles are advertised in London, Frankfurt, Paris, Dubai, Doha, Stockholm, Milan and outside EMEA [R1-S05][R1-S06][R1-S07][R1-S08][R5-S16][R5-S17].
- **Clients:** Institutional investors (pension funds, endowments, foundations, sovereign wealth funds, insurers) and wealth intermediaries (private banks, wealth managers, advisers, platforms, multi-managers) [R1-S20][R1-S17].
- **Who decides on the client side:** Varies by client type: see each team.
- **Investment needs:** Varies by client type: see each team.
- **Products and strategies:** Goldman lists 'fixed income, equities, liquid alternatives, private equity, private credit, infrastructure and real estate' [R1-S10].
- **Distribution channels:** Direct institutional coverage, consultant relations, third-party wealth intermediaries, insurance and retirement channels [R4-S09].
- **Commercial process:** Not one process. Institutional business is usually won through consultant-led tenders and long due diligence; wealth business through approval by a gatekeeper and then adoption by advisers. [Supported inference]
- **Specialist dependencies:** Portfolio management, product specialists, marketing, compliance, operations, legal, performance measurement and risk, accounting and billing [R1-S10][R1-S01].
- **How the business model differs:** CSG does not manage money. It is how the investment teams' strategies reach clients and how clients' needs reach the investment teams. Goldman does not disclose revenue, assets, flows or headcount for CSG or for any EMEA client team [R2-S01].
- **Languages (job-description evidence only):** None at group level. Requirements are set team by team in job descriptions.
- **Recruitment evidence:** The 2027 London Summer Analyst listing is filed under this group and contains no team-specific text [R1-S02]. The 2026 cycle used sub-track titles such as 'Client Solutions Group, UK Institutional Sales' (search result only) [R1-S31]. An applicant may apply to at most four business and location combinations a year [R1-S02].
- **Unresolved questions:** How London applicants are allocated to a team. Whether the Client Coverage Group sits inside CSG or beside it. Whether London teams use 'CSG' to mean the sales side of a team.

### UK Institutional `T-uk-inst`

- **Evidence status:** Supported inference
- **Where the name comes from:** The former intern's label. The 2026-cycle London listing was titled 'Client Solutions Group, UK Institutional Sales' (search result only; page expired) [R1-S31]. Senior public titles: 'head of the UK and Ireland institutional business', then 'co-head of EMEA Institutional Client Coverage' [R6-S05][R6-S02].
- **Kind of unit:** Client segment within the UK grouping
- **In one paragraph:** Coverage of UK institutional investors. The former intern describes pension funds as dominant, with endowments and foundations and sovereign wealth funds also covered. Public evidence of named UK clients is almost entirely defined benefit pension schemes reached through OCIO or fiduciary mandates, plus older Local Government Pension Scheme mandates.
- **Former intern's account:** His own team, on the sales side. 'The main team' and the one most likely to be hiring. Pension funds dominate; his project was client research on endowments and foundations. [Unverified account]
- **What public sources establish:** Goldman's EMEA institutional marketing defines the institutional business as pension funds, endowments, foundations, sovereign wealth funds and insurers [R1-S20]. The co-head of EMEA Institutional Client Coverage is quoted in the Shell OCIO announcement [R3-S04][R6-S02]. A head of EMEA defined contribution within CSG was reported appointed in June 2025 (search result only) [R6-S26]. Public UK mandates outside OCIO are sparse: a Border to Coast emerging-markets equity sleeve (2023) and older local-authority mandates, some later terminated [R7-S44][R7-S46]. No public source names a current head of a 'UK Institutional sales' team. [Not publicly established]
- **Clients:** Defined benefit pension schemes, defined contribution master trusts and providers, Local Government Pension Scheme funds and pools, endowments, foundations and charities, and official institutions. Which of these the London team actually covers beyond pension schemes is not publicly established.
- **Who decides on the client side:** Trustee boards and their investment sub-committees, the scheme's in-house investment staff or chief investment officer where one exists, the sponsoring employer on some decisions, and the investment consultant who advises the trustees and often runs the selection. For LGPS assets, increasingly the pool rather than the individual fund [R3-S21].
- **Investment needs:** For closed defined benefit schemes: paying pensions as they fall due, hedging interest-rate and inflation risk, generating cash flow, and reaching an endgame (insurer buyout or run-on). Aggregate funding is strong: the PPF 7800 funding ratio was 133.7% at end October 2026 [R3-S29]. For defined contribution: default-fund design under cost constraints and a push toward private markets [R3-S20][R3-S23].
- **Products and strategies:** Liability-driven and cashflow-driven investment, credit and fixed income, multi-asset, equity, private markets, and OCIO where the client wants to delegate. Goldman cited about $300bn globally in LDI and CDI in September 2025 [R3-S04].
- **Distribution channels:** Direct coverage of schemes and coverage of the consultants who advise them.
- **Commercial process:** Typically: a consultant or trustee identifies a need, a shortlist is drawn, managers answer a request for proposal and due-diligence questionnaire, a final presentation is held, then legal negotiation, onboarding and transition. Cycles are long and the consultant's view of the manager matters throughout. [Supported inference]
- **Specialist dependencies:** Consultant relations; the UK LDI and CDI pensions solutions team in fixed income [R3-S13]; the OCIO and Multi-Asset Solutions teams; product specialists; request-for-proposal and marketing teams; legal and client implementation.
- **How the business model differs:** Few clients, large tickets, slow decisions, formal governance and published advisers. Revenue arrives as a management fee on a mandate or fund holding, at institutional rates. The structural trend (schemes maturing, buying out with insurers, or delegating to OCIO) means the same client may shrink, leave to an insurer, or hand everything to one provider.
- **Languages (job-description evidence only):** No UK institutional job description with a language requirement was read. [Not publicly established]
- **Recruitment evidence:** The 2026 London campus track carried the title 'UK Institutional Sales' (search result only) [R1-S31]. The former intern says it is the team most likely to be hiring. [Unverified account]
- **Unresolved questions:** Current head of UK institutional sales. Whether the team covers endowments, charities, LGPS, DC and sovereign institutions in practice. Whether it is split into sales and relationship management as described.

### UK Third Party Wealth (TPW) `T-uk-tpw`

- **Evidence status:** Verified
- **Where the name comes from:** Goldman Sachs's own name: a job advert refers to the 'UK Third Party Wealth (TPW) Sales Team' [R1-S17]; another, seen through an aggregator, to the 'UK & Ireland Third Party Wealth team' [R4-S08]. A press release names the 'EMEA Third Party Wealth Business' [R4-S01].
- **Kind of unit:** Client segment within the UK grouping
- **In one paragraph:** Sells Goldman Sachs Asset Management funds, exchange-traded funds and alternatives to other firms that then use them for their own clients: private banks, wealth managers, financial advisers and multi-managers. The client is an intermediary, not the end investor.
- **Former intern's account:** Sells Goldman funds to other wealth managers and private banks, who offer them to their own private clients. A friend interned on the relationship side. [Unverified account] His named example of a fund sold to another bank's private bank is not publicly established. [Not publicly established]
- **What public sources establish:** The UK TPW Sales Team 'is responsible for new business development' with 'private banks, wealth managers, financial advisors and multi-managers' [R1-S17]. The UK & Ireland team's stated clients are private banks, wealth managers, fund of funds and independent financial advisers, offered traditional and alternative strategies as funds, ETFs or separately managed accounts [R4-S08]. A UK head of ETF distribution is named publicly [R6-S31]. The EMEA head from 2021 left in spring 2026 and no successor had been named in the sources found [R4-S02]. A formal split into sales and relationship management is not publicly established. [Not publicly established]
- **Clients:** Private banks, wealth managers and discretionary fund managers, advice networks and independent financial advisers, multi-managers and funds of funds, and the platforms through which they deal.
- **Who decides on the client side:** The fund selector or research team (the gatekeeper), the investment committee that approves the buy list or model portfolio, then individual portfolio managers and advisers who decide whether to use an approved fund. The end investor rarely chooses the fund directly.
- **Investment needs:** Funds that fit a model portfolio or buy list, at a share-class price that passes value assessment, with reliable reporting and someone who can explain performance to advisers. Under the Consumer Duty the distributor must be able to show fair value for retail customers [R4-S31].
- **Products and strategies:** UCITS funds, active and index UCITS ETFs (active equity range from April 2025, further fixed-income ETFs in April 2026) [R4-S01][R4-S17], and evergreen private-markets funds and ELTIFs for eligible investors [R4-S19][R4-S20]. No Goldman Sachs Long-Term Asset Fund or UK model portfolio service was identified. [Not publicly established]
- **Distribution channels:** Gatekeeper approval, buy lists and model portfolios, fund platforms, and adviser-facing sales support.
- **Commercial process:** Research and gatekeeper meetings, due diligence, approval, making the share class available on the platforms the firm uses, then adviser-by-adviser adoption and ongoing monitoring. Approval is permission to buy; it does not produce assets by itself. [Supported inference]
- **Specialist dependencies:** Product specialists and client portfolio managers, the ETF distribution team, the Third Party Wealth Alternatives team [R4-S11], marketing, and compliance for financial promotions.
- **How the business model differs:** Many clients, smaller tickets, flows that build gradually and can reverse quickly. Revenue is the fund's management fee on assets that arrive only when advisers allocate. Buying power is concentrating in model portfolio services and consolidated wealth groups, so fewer decisions move more money.
- **Languages (job-description evidence only):** 'Native English speaker is essential'; no other language required [R1-S17].
- **Recruitment evidence:** A UK TPW sales-support analyst advert (closed, undated) [R1-S17] and an experienced-hire vice president advert seen through aggregators [R4-S08]. No campus evidence specific to this team.
- **Unresolved questions:** Head of the UK & Ireland team. Successor to the EMEA head. Whether a separate relationship-management side exists.

### OCIO / fiduciary management `T-ocio`

- **Evidence status:** Verified
- **Where the name comes from:** Goldman Sachs's own names: 'UK fiduciary management business', 'International OCIO and UK Fiduciary Management Team', 'Outsourced Chief Investment Officer business', 'EMEA OCIO Institutional Business' [R3-S16][R3-S01][R3-S10][R3-S11].
- **Kind of unit:** Delegated-portfolio business within Multi-Asset Solutions (an investing group); global
- **In one paragraph:** The business that takes delegated responsibility for running all or part of an institution's portfolio. It is global, not UK-only, and it sits in Multi-Asset Solutions, an investment group, not in a regional sales team. Client coverage works alongside it.
- **Former intern's account:** One of three UK sub-teams. 'Pretty sure' it exists only in the UK team. Goldman can bring the client's in-house investment team into the firm. Recently won an award. 'Already over-hired'. [Unverified account]
- **What public sources establish:** Not UK-only: Goldman reported $480bn of OCIO assets under supervision at 31 March 2026 and '$540+ billion' at 30 June 2026, with large US mandates and stated growth in the Netherlands, Germany and Switzerland [R3-S09][R8-S22][R3-S10]. [Conflicting evidence] The fiduciary and OCIO teams sit within Multi-Asset Solutions [R6-S18][R1-S15], supported by a team of more than 300 people that was still growing in November 2025 [R3-S07]. UK history: a leader hired from a consultant in late 2021 [R3-S16], Short Brothers (£1.6bn, 2022) [R3-S15], BAE Systems (about £23bn, 2023, in-house team transferred) [R3-S01], Shell entities (about $40bn across countries, 2025) [R3-S04]. Team transfer is reported only in some of the largest deals [R7-S04]. Fee rates are not disclosed. [Not publicly established] 'Over-hired' has no public support. [Not publicly established]
- **Clients:** Corporate defined benefit pension schemes of all sizes; also a captive insurer and, in the United States, defined contribution plan advisory. Public UK names include the BAE Systems schemes, Shell UK pension entities, the Short Brothers Common Investment Fund, the Calor plan and the Northern Foods scheme (see the mandates register).
- **Who decides on the client side:** Trustee boards, advised by an independent consultant or evaluator who runs the tender; the sponsoring employer where it bears the cost or its in-house team is affected. In the public UK cases the advisers were Redington, Isio, PwC and Barnett Waddingham [R3-S02][R3-S04][R3-S15].
- **Investment needs:** Governance capacity the trustees do not have in house, faster implementation, access to managers and private markets, integrated liability hedging, and a credible path to the scheme's endgame. Goldman's stated view is that sponsors increasingly ask whether running a pension scheme is core business [R3-S07].
- **Products and strategies:** Delegated management: strategy advice (in full fiduciary management), asset allocation, manager selection using internal and external managers, liability hedging and reporting [R3-S15][R3-S08].
- **Distribution channels:** Competitive tender. UK trust-based schemes must invite bids from at least three unconnected providers before fiduciary managers run 20% or more of assets [R3-S24].
- **Commercial process:** Tender run by a third-party evaluator, scored proposals and standardised performance data, trustee decision, then a long transition of assets and, in a few very large cases, of people.
- **Specialist dependencies:** Multi-Asset Solutions portfolio managers, the External Investing Group for manager selection, LDI and CDI specialists, transition management, legal and operations.
- **How the business model differs:** The fee is for running the whole portfolio, usually a low rate on a large base, with underlying managers' fees charged separately. A public UK scheme report (scheme name withheld) shows an asset-based fiduciary fee on the return-seeking and cashflow-driven portfolios with the LDI manager invoicing separately [R3-S17]. In Goldman's filings, advisory and OCIO alternative accounts averaged 17 basis points in 2025, a firm-wide blend and not a mandate price [R2-S01]. One appointment can be very large, but each is rare, slow and re-tendered.
- **Languages (job-description evidence only):** None found for UK roles. The OCIO Insurance advert in The Hague states none in the text read [R1-S15].
- **Recruitment evidence:** Senior hiring continued in September 2025 [R3-S07]. A 'Client Relationship Manager (OCIO)' London title was seen in search results only [R1-S33]. No analyst-level campus evidence.
- **Unresolved questions:** Goldman's UK-only OCIO assets and market rank. Its OCIO fee rates. Whether CSG summer analysts are placed with OCIO client coverage. Which of two 2026 awards the former intern saw.

### Consultant Relations `T-consultant`

- **Evidence status:** Verified
- **Where the name comes from:** Goldman Sachs's own name: 'Consultant Relations' and 'Global Consultant Relations' [R1-S21][R6-S25].
- **Kind of unit:** Function: coverage of investment consultants
- **In one paragraph:** Covers the investment consulting firms that advise institutional investors, rate managers and run selections. It does not win mandates directly; it builds the consultants' understanding of the firm so that sales teams are considered.
- **Former intern's account:** One of the three functions inside CSG: 'covering the investment consultants who steer clients toward managers'. [Unverified account]
- **What public sources establish:** An older London advert describes the team as working with the regional institutional sales teams and creating 'a pipeline of business for the sales teams', with UK and continental European travel [R1-S21]. A managing director was reported as joining in September 2024 as head of international, global consultant relations, based in London [R6-S25]. A Goldman advert lists 'institutional, third-party wealth, insurance and consultant relations teams' side by side [R5-S42]. Whether the function formally sits inside CSG today is not established from a primary source read directly.
- **Clients:** Investment consulting firms: for UK pensions, firms such as WTW, Mercer, Aon, LCP, Hymans Robertson, Isio, XPS, Redington and Barnett Waddingham.
- **Who decides on the client side:** Consultants' manager-research teams (who rate strategies) and field consultants (who advise specific clients).
- **Investment needs:** Deep, consistent information on strategies, people and process; early notice of changes; access to portfolio managers.
- **Products and strategies:** No product of its own. It supports ratings across the firm's strategies.
- **Distribution channels:** Research meetings, data submissions to consultant databases, strategy reviews.
- **Commercial process:** Maintain ratings, respond to research requests, brief consultants on changes, and pass intelligence on searches to the sales teams.
- **Specialist dependencies:** Portfolio managers and product specialists for research meetings; the request-for-proposal team for data.
- **How the business model differs:** No direct revenue. Its value shows up as shortlists and ratings that make a sale possible. The consulting sector is consolidating, which concentrates this influence in fewer firms [R3-S34].
- **Languages (job-description evidence only):** 'A second European language' was listed as an advantage in the older advert [R1-S21].
- **Recruitment evidence:** Older associate advert (undated); vice president and analyst titles seen in search results only [R1-S34].
- **Unresolved questions:** Current structure and exact place within CSG. Size of the London team.

- **Kind of unit:** Product-line client business (global)
- **In one paragraph:** A client business organised around a product, not a region: money market funds and short-duration strategies for clients with operating or strategic cash. It has global leadership shared with Insurance Asset Management and an EMEA sales seat in London.
- **Former intern's account:** A product line with its own team 'because the product is strong'. He did not know how it is split. He said an English-only candidate could go there, then said everyone in it speaks French. [Unverified account]
- **What public sources establish:** 'Our Liquidity Solutions team oversees $1.2+ trillion in money market and short-term assets' as at 30 September 2026 (global) [R5-S01]; firm-wide liquidity assets under supervision were $1,051bn at the same date [R2-S02]. Clients: 'financial institution, hedge fund, institutional, corporate, and wealth management clients' [R5-S01]. A London 'EMEA Liquidity Solutions Sales (UK Corporates)' seat covers UK corporate and insurance clients (search summary) [R5-S09]. No evidence that French is required: the one French-speaker advert found belongs to the French sales team. [Not publicly established] Its placement inside CSG is the former intern's account; public sources show its own global client-business head.
- **Clients:** Corporate treasurers, financial institutions, hedge funds, private equity and venture firms, public institutions, insurers, pension schemes holding collateral, and wealth clients.
- **Who decides on the client side:** Treasurers and treasury committees working to a board-approved investment policy; chief financial officers; collateral and operations managers at funds and schemes. [Supported inference]
- **Investment needs:** Safety of capital first, same-day or next-day access second, yield third. Counterparty diversification, credit ratings and operational ease (portals, cut-off times) often decide the choice. [Supported inference]
- **Products and strategies:** Money market funds: GS US$ Liquid Reserves and GS Euro Liquid Reserves (low-volatility net asset value), GS US$ Treasury Liquid Reserves (public debt constant net asset value); short-duration accounts and funds; fixed income ETFs; the Mosaic portal [R5-S01].
- **Distribution channels:** Direct treasury coverage and dealing portals.
- **Commercial process:** Onboarding and counterparty approval, then daily subscriptions and redemptions with no sales event attached. The 'mandate' is permission to place cash; the balance moves every day.
- **Specialist dependencies:** Money market portfolio managers and credit analysts; operations and portal support.
- **How the business model differs:** Thin fee on a very large, very mobile balance. The investor earns the portfolio yield net of the fund charge; the manager earns that charge on average balances. Firm-wide, liquidity products earned an average 14 basis points in 2025 [R2-S01]. Balances can leave in a day for reasons unrelated to service.
- **Languages (job-description evidence only):** None seen in the UK Corporates advert summary [R5-S09]. French requirement: not publicly established.
- **Recruitment evidence:** Experienced-hire London postings only; no student-programme evidence specific to liquidity.
- **Unresolved questions:** Internal split; whether CSG summer analysts are placed here; EMEA head.

### Insurance `T-ins`

- **Evidence status:** Verified
- **Where the name comes from:** Goldman Sachs's own names: 'Insurance Asset Management' and, in advert titles, 'Insurance Client Solutions Group' [R5-S02][R5-S21].
- **Kind of unit:** Client vertical (global)
- **In one paragraph:** A global client vertical for insurance companies' own balance-sheet assets. It has named global heads and seats in London and Frankfurt, and was extended in Europe by the NN Investment Partners acquisition.
- **Former intern's account:** Its own client base, mentioned as an afterthought. Where it sits is unclear. [Unverified account]
- **What public sources establish:** Goldman Sachs Asset Management states it manages '$651 billion in general account assets on behalf of insurance clients' as at 31 December 2025 [R5-S02]. Its offer is partial to full outsourcing across fixed income, alternatives and equities, plus advice on asset-liability management, strategic asset allocation and capital-efficient strategies [R5-S02]. 'Insurance Client Solutions Group' roles have been advertised in London and Frankfurt (search summaries) [R5-S21][R5-S22]. A CSG advert lists insurance beside institutional and third-party wealth as a peer channel (search summary) [R5-S42]. Whether EMEA insurance staff report regionally or to the global vertical is not established. [Not publicly established]
- **Clients:** Life, health, property and casualty, and reinsurance companies [R5-S21].
- **Who decides on the client side:** The insurer's chief investment officer and chief financial officer, with actuarial, risk and capital-management teams involved in every decision.
- **Investment needs:** Assets that match liabilities, earn spread, and use regulatory capital efficiently. The rulebook is changing: amended EU Solvency II rules apply from 30 January 2027 [R5-S39]; the UK regulator has consulted on faster access to matching-adjustment benefits [R5-S38]. In Goldman's 2026 survey of 434 insurance investment and finance chiefs, 62% planned to increase private-asset allocations [R5-S03].
- **Products and strategies:** Investment-grade fixed income, private credit and asset-backed finance, and full or partial outsourcing of the general account [R5-S02].
- **Distribution channels:** Direct coverage by insurance specialists.
- **Commercial process:** Solution design around the insurer's balance sheet, with constraints on capital charges, accounting treatment, book yield and realised gains written into guidelines.
- **Specialist dependencies:** Insurance strategists, the OCIO Insurance team within Multi-Asset Solutions [R1-S15], fixed income and private credit teams.
- **How the business model differs:** Large, sticky, low-fee fixed-income mandates where the manager is judged on yield, capital use and accounting outcomes as much as on return against an index.
- **Languages (job-description evidence only):** Not read in a job description. [Not publicly established]
- **Recruitment evidence:** Experienced-hire postings in London and Frankfurt (search summaries) [R5-S21][R5-S22].
- **Unresolved questions:** Reporting structure in EMEA; EMEA head; whether CSG summer analysts are placed here.

# Appendix C: Mandates and commercial events

### BAE Systems Pension Scheme and BAE Systems Executive Pension Scheme `M-R7-01`

- **Evidence status:** Verified
- **Client type:** Corporate defined benefit pension schemes
- **Country:** United Kingdom
- **Event date:** 2023-09-06 (announced); transition expected towards end of 2023; scheme SIPs updated 11 July 2024
- **Kind of event:** OCIO appointment
- **Strategy:** Outsourced chief investment officer for the schemes' DB assets, including liability-driven and cashflow-driven portfolios; in-house investment team (BAE Systems Pension Funds Investment Management) moved to GSAM and continues to serve the schemes
- **Amount as disclosed:** Approximately £23 billion
- **What the amount measures:** UK defined benefit scheme assets handed over for management at announcement. Not a fee figure and not a statement of fee-paying AUM by strategy.
- **Stated rationale:** Sponsor: 'reducing the cost and improving the efficiency of asset management are essential'. Trustee chair credited the in-house team's stewardship and framed the move as a long-term solution. Selected after a 'highly competitive tender process'.
- **Consultant involvement:** Redington (trustees' strategic investment adviser since 2021; advised on the deal and oversees implementation). Travers Smith (trustees' lawyers). PwC advised the sponsor. Gallagher is named as the trustee's investment adviser in the 2026 implementation statement.
- **Decision-makers:** Trustees of both schemes (chair Andrew Gallagher); sponsor group finance director Brad Greve quoted
- **Public attribution to a GS team:** Press release quotes Ed Francis as Head of International OCIO and UK Fiduciary Management, with David Solomon and Marc Nachmann. No source attributes the win to a sales or coverage team or to any other individual.
- **Notes:** Described by Goldman as the largest OCIO mandate awarded in the UK to that date. Still in force: the scheme's implementation statement for the year to 31 March 2026 calls GSAM 'the Scheme's OCIO'. The trustee retains a separate investment adviser, so OCIO did not remove independent oversight. Number of staff transferred is not public.
- **Sources:** R7-S01, R7-S02, R7-S03, R7-S04, R7-S05, R7-S06, R7-S07

### Various pension entities and a captive insurance company related to Shell plc (UK, Germany, Bermuda and other locations); advisory for North American plans `M-R7-02`

- **Evidence status:** Verified
- **Client type:** Corporate pension funds and captive insurer
- **Country:** United Kingdom / Germany / other Europe / North America (advisory)
- **Event date:** 2025-09-09 (announced); transitions expected to complete later in 2025
- **Kind of event:** OCIO appointment
- **Strategy:** OCIO for international pension plan assets in Europe (includes LDI and CDI); investment advisory services for North American plans
- **Amount as disclosed:** $40 billion in total; of which about $15.6 billion (about £11.5bn) UK and $2.8 billion Germany
- **What the amount measures:** Pension plan and captive assets covered by the mandates at announcement. The rest of the $40bn is not itemised. No asset figure is given for the North American advisory element. Not fee-paying AUM by strategy.
- **Stated rationale:** Marc Nachmann: asset owners 'increasingly want differentiated alpha, holistic total portfolio advice and customized portfolio solutions'. Each fund 'set clear objectives and selection criteria'. Shell spokesperson: Shell acted as coordinator; decisions were made by the individual funds.
- **Consultant involvement:** Isio (oversaw the competitive tender)
- **Decision-makers:** Trustees of each fund, deciding separately
- **Public attribution to a GS team:** Press release quotes Chloe Kipling, co-head of EMEA Institutional Client Coverage, and Marc Nachmann. mallowstreet reports 'some staff will move to GSAM'. No further team attribution is public.
- **Notes:** The Dutch Shell fund (SSPF) is not part of this: it appointed BlackRock in 2024. That shows one sponsor's schemes can choose different OCIO providers. Completion of the transition has not been separately confirmed in a source read for this register.
- **Sources:** R7-S08, R7-S09, R7-S10, R7-S11, R7-S12, R7-S24
